title: Consequences of Disobedience
english: He performs extraordinary powers that we cannot even begin to endure, and this has sparked zeal and envy within us. The deaf obey when called, and the blind see when they turn towards him, having received their sight from him. The lame ask for feet, having borrowed hands and a tongue from him. Through him, the beds of the sick are emptied, and there is no distinction between the healthy and the sick. Lepers are cleansed through him, and there is no need for doctors or medicine. He does not cease to speak out against this holy place and the law.

We have heard him say that Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the customs given to us by Moses (Matthew 24:2, Acts 6:14). You are rightly called false witnesses and slanderers because you speak the truth as if it were not true, and you call the prophecies about him blasphemies against God. Whose voice, whose prophecy, whose preaching is this? Who inspired Isaiah and Micah to speak these words? Because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will be like a watchtower (Micah 3:12). The daughter of Zion will be left like a tent in a vineyard and like a watchtower in a cucumber field (Isaiah 1:8). Who inspired David to say these things? Remember, Lord, the day of Jerusalem, the day when the sons of Edom said, 'Empty, empty, until the foundation in her' (Psalm 137:7).

The consequences of disobedience are severe, and God will empty and purge his people until they return to their foundation. Moses, like Stephen, warned of the curses that would befall the nation if they strayed from God's path. These curses, which have now come to pass, provide a clear view of their origins and demonstrate the consequences of rejecting God's gifts. The events that have occurred to the Jewish people are a testament to the truth of Moses' words. If you go astray, God will add seven plagues according to your sins, since you rejected the seven gifts of the Spirit. The last state of the people became worse than the first. And I will send against you the beasts of the earth, which are the nations, because they were previously ignorant, worshiping idols in the form of beasts and four-footed animals (Leviticus 26:22, Deuteronomy 32:24). David said that those who make and trust in idols are like them (Psalm 115:8). Now God has sent the nations against them, which will devour them, destroy their livestock, and make them few. And your ways will be desolate. For each of these things, the nations have taken control, according to what is perceived and what is understood. The temple, obviously, is the house that will be built but not lived in. We may also consider the vineyard to be the vineyard of Christ. God did not limit the threats to Moses to these, but also added more severe ones. He says: 'You will take a wife, and another man will have her. You will build a house, and you will not live in it. You will plant a vineyard, and you will not harvest it. Your ox will be slaughtered before you, and you will not eat from it.' He threatened many other things, and did not hide the reason for these things, but brought it forward with many threats, which are connected to what was said earlier. 'Your life will be hanging before your eyes, and you will fear day and night, and you will not trust your life. In the morning you will say, 'How will it be evening?' And in the evening you will say, 'How will it be morning?' And because of the fear in your heart, and the things you will see, you will be afraid.

The consequences of disobedience will be severe, and the people will suffer greatly. Their ways will be desolate, and they will be taken over by the nations. This is not just a matter of perception, but also of understanding.

title: Theology of the Cross
english: For Christ was from them, the vine of our life; but we harvest his grape, we mix his wine, and we drink his sweet wine. Your calf is slaughtered before you, and you will not eat from it; for theirs is the sacrifice of Christ, they brought the heavenly calf to the altar, but also our dinner, our table. And why? Because they bore unbelief, they brought ignorance instead of knowledge, and in the time of theology, they slipped into blasphemy.

They dressed the bride but did not accept the bridegroom; they crowned the bridal chamber and denied the wedding. And while the cross was being prepared, the elements were being shaken, but they did not change. This is what followed: 'And your life will be hanging before your eyes' (Genesis 27:3). Who is life? Christ says: 'I am the way, the life, and the truth' (John 14:6). And where does it hang? On the wood of the cross. For he who hung the earth with a word hangs on the wood, in which he is borne while bearing, in which he is hung while hanging, in which he is lifted while lifting: 'For when I am lifted up' (John 12:32), he says, 'I will draw all to myself.' And 'you will fear day and night, and you will not trust your life' (Genesis 37:9). Therefore, unbelief has become the cause of fear.

'You will fear day and night'; for day and night are the same, because 'from the sixth hour, darkness prevailed over the whole earth' (Mark 15:33). And it will be on that day, there will be no light; and cold and frost will be; the day is great, it will be known to the Lord; not day nor night; and towards evening, there will be light; and living water will come out of Jerusalem; half of it to the first sea, and half of it to the last sea; these things happened sensibly and intelligibly.

'On that day, there will be no light'; for the sun was darkened at noon, and ignorance was poured out upon the hearts of the Jews. 'Cold and frost will be.' Peter testifies to this, warming himself by the charcoal during the height of the winter hour. But there was cold and frost, because the love of God had grown cold among the Jews; for they would not have received the one coming from Him as Savior and Redeemer, but they crucified Him. 'The day is great.' How could it not be great, in which Adam was remade, sin was abolished, death was destroyed, the vessel received the treasure, the shepherd received the sheep, and the merchant received the pearl? 'It will be known to God.' For how could He, who knows all things, not especially know that day, in which He gave His only-begotten Son for sacrifice? 'Not day nor night,' because the course of the day did not reach night. 'Towards evening, there will be light,' because after the ninth hour the darkness ceased. Thus, the same thing became both night and day.

'And living water will come out of Jerusalem.' From where? From the side of the living one; for just as Eve was formed, there the church is likewise formed. 'The half of it into the first sea'—that is a sign of baptism. 'And the half of it into the last sea'—this is clearly a sign of repentance. For the tears of repentance are a remnant of the gift of baptism, a clear proof: for one who has not been baptized repents in vain if he does not run to be baptized; in vain he offers prayer, in vain he asks for forgiveness, in vain he sheds tears. For without baptism, the forgiveness of sins is not granted. But one who has been baptized has effective repentance: he weeps and is loosed, he sighs and mourns and prays, and he is immediately cleansed.

But because he goes out to hear the rest of the law's proclamation: 'In the morning you will say, "How can it be evening?" (Zechariah 14:7) And in the evening you will say, "How can it be morning?" (Zechariah 14:7)' From where? 'From the fear of your heart, because of the things you will fear, and from the sights of the eyes you will see' (Zechariah 14:4). Because of the signs and the wonders that were being done during the time of the cross—the earth shaking, the sun fleeing, the heaven hiding, the rocks splitting, the tombs opening—those who were terrified and agitated were compelled to say to one another: 'How can it be evening?' so that we might bring life down from the cross and hide from the earth the one from heaven...

title: Stephen’s Vision of the Open Heavens
english: Let us enclose the immortal One in the tomb and bring forth the wonder from within, so that these frightful objects may be a source of fear to us.

But even after doing all this, they did not escape their goal; on the contrary, their attempted deed turned against them, and they found themselves in a situation where they had to ask, 'How could it possibly become morning?'

This question arose because the events of the resurrection night were fearful to behold again: they saw the tomb as a bridal chamber, the grave sealed, the corpse rising with life, the soldiers like young men, the women bringing myrrh, angels guarding the linen cloths, and one sitting upon the stone as a herald of the resurrection.

Then they said again, 'How could it possibly become morning?'—in order that they might give silver to the soldiers, corrupt Pilate, steal the truth by deceit, and claim, 'His disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping.'

These schemes are in accordance with the law and Moses, yet in each instance, it is God who bears witness to the ignorant people, as Stephen the theologian rebuked them, and they called him a blasphemer.

The high priest asked, 'If these things are truly so?'—as if to say, 'You do not even know how things stand!' 'Did you not devise the deceit?' 'Did you not hire those who strike together?' 'Do not the witnesses of deceit pay you?'
But he added, 'No, we have need of falsehood and hypocrisy, and we need deceit toward the trap that has been set before us, just as we sold Joseph, murdered Nabothai, and crucified Christ.'

Stephen, having found an opportunity for teaching, poured many salvific things into the ears of the people, and he concluded his rhetoric by saying, 'You are hard-hearted and uncircumcised in heart and ears, and you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did, and you.'

He began by saying, 'Brothers and fathers, hear me,' but he noted that while they were descended from the noble Abraham, they had become wicked, and while they were branches of the good root, they had become disorderly and hard.

Isaiah had urged them to say to those who hated and abhorred them, 'Let the name of the Lord be glorified' (Isaiah 66:5), but they compelled Stephen to speak against his judgment, and he called them brothers and fathers, lest they think he was accusing them as enemies.
However, they did not endure his sayings, and they gnashed their teeth in fury, just as it was said of them, 'Their teeth are swords and arrows, and their tongue is a sharpened blade' (Psalm 57:4).
But Stephen did not fix his gaze on them; instead, he lifted his eyes to God, left the earth behind, and rushed toward the heavenly courts, crying aloud, 'See, I behold the heavens opened!'

This means that the blessing is shared, the path is level for all, and the gateway stands wide for those who desire to enter; the valiant athlete must strive promptly, using his weapons and displaying the full measure of his strength, for the Judge of the contest is watching and holding the crowns and prizes in his hand, ready to bestow them.

'See, I behold the heavens opened!' And who opened them? He did not leave the one who wishes to know in ignorance; therefore, Stephen cried out, 'The Son of Man stands at the right hand of the Power of God,' meaning the eternal Word of God who took on flesh.

For since the Son of God became the Son of Man, and the One who came from the Father, born of the Virgin, took His stand upon earth and heaven as a boundary, the dividing wall of hostility has been dismantled, and the barrier removed, making the rights of citizenship common to angels and to humanity alike—if humanity chooses to claim them.

Thus, it is permitted for those who live upon the earth to engage in heavenly warfare: to feel the weakness of the flesh below, to be strengthened by the Spirit above, to be one with the clay in their humble condition, and yet to be one with God in the life of the mind.

These things Stephen was indeed proclaiming as theology, but the cries of that spiritual teaching were chaotic, and the shouts were passed from one to another, while stones were hurled from slings at those who upheld the holy laws.
